claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: I looked at the bank the bank balance sheet is like a set of portfolios, asset portfolios, liability portfolios with different speeds
claims.claim: Treating a bank balance sheet as a set of asset and liability portfolios with different speeds (repricing/duration) lets you manage net interest margin as a portfolio problem.
claims.indicator: asset and liability portfolio duration and repricing speed
claims.testable: partly - ALM mismatch measures are standard

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: I got all their historical reports to see if they were accurate
claims.claim: Before subscribing, Prince checked the research firm's past published reports for accuracy, a simple track-record verification of a forecaster.
claims.testable: yes - compare past calls to outcomes

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: the economist understanding how the economy works, the trader understanding markets, flows, risk, reward, and then the integration of those two
claims.claim: Bridgewater's edge is integrating economic understanding with market understanding (flows, risk, reward) into one system.

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: laying it out the way you think it works to the point that you've literally coded into the computer and now you're going to live with it
claims.claim: Systemising a view by coding it into rules and then trading it forces accountability and honest evaluation of outcomes, instead of adjusting the story after the fact.
claims.indicator: coded fundamental systems (interest rate, stock, gold systems)
claims.testable: yes - rules are explicit and testable

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: businesses are really comprised of two things. One is like an operating margin and the other is a bet on the markets.
claims.claim: Companies carry hidden market exposures (e.g. a jeweler is long gold), so profits blend operating performance and market bets; risk-management plans separate and hedge the latter.
claims.indicator: business profit split into operating margin vs embedded market exposure
claims.conditions: Firms that accept market bets to boost short-term profit
claims.testable: yes - decompose firm returns by factor exposure

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: when the dollar was super strong like they were doing layoffs and they were getting hurt because the Japanese could undercut them because of the dollar
claims.claim: A strong dollar hurts US exporters like Caterpillar because foreign competitors can undercut them, causing layoffs.
claims.indicator: US dollar strength vs manufacturing employment
claims.testable: partly - FX vs exporter earnings measurable

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: 3% unemployment when Boston had an 18% unemployment rate and then all of a sudden oil prices go down and that everything flip-flops
claims.claim: Oil-dependent regions (Tulsa) boom or bust with oil prices regardless of individual performance, so local economies are whipped by commodity prices.

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: get off the planet get above it and you could take any market in the world and go long or short
claims.claim: Moving from a single-market exposure to a global long/short mandate lets you exploit any market and avoid being a sitting duck to one price.

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: if we have a deflationary depression it everything's going to go down together
claims.claim: Kodak's CIO worried that a diversified portfolio would fall together in a deflationary depression; a small allocation of long-duration (25-year) bonds could deliver the price action of five times the capital as a hedge.
claims.testable: yes - bond returns in deflation episodes

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: it was 25 year duration implemented with futures two two times two and a half times leverage and 10-year bond futures we could shift the duration from uh 40 years all the way down to zero
claims.claim: The first alpha-overlay mandate was implemented with futures: 25-year target duration, 2-2.5x leverage, duration flexible from 40 years to zero, currency exposure plus or minus 100% and any country, combining liability hedge and alpha.

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: we pulled data from the Federal Reserve bulletins on railroad bond yields back to the 1860s
claims.claim: To answer the long-duration question the team assembled bond-yield and yield-curve data back to the 1860s, producing a landmark study; long history is key to testing deflation hedges.

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: Just think about what is the right answer and and think about that from a st from first principles
claims.claim: Derive answers from the basic mechanics of how the world works, independent of what others do, because convention settles in.

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: if you're actually right, then in time the world comes to you
claims.claim: Being alone and radically different from consensus is acceptable if truly right: the world eventually converges, which was the basis of Bridgewater's growth.

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: your power is in what you don't know and and and your risk is in pursuing what you know
claims.claim: Risk comes from what you do not know you are missing; stating humility explicitly and combining people with different capabilities provides a window into blind spots.

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: the markets are a pure meritocracy because it's you know there nobody's name goes on a trade
claims.claim: Markets are zero-sum and returns are the objective standard of right or wrong, so an organisation without internal meritocracy will not compete.

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: policy makers have managed to finally kind of bring things into a reasonable balance. And just as they're achieving this reasonable balance, not just in the United States, but across a lot of countries, you now have this geopolitical chaos
claims.claim: After five years of imbalances (COVID, overheating, tight money), policy makers had restored balance across countries, but geopolitical chaos (tariffs, boycotts) now threatens it: a clash of stability vs instability.

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: this new mode of operating that we call modern mercantalism which is if you go back through the last many decades the the the prevailing theory was globalization and free markets
claims.claim: Globalisation created imbalances that produced leaders favouring government involvement, an inward focus and competition instead of cooperation (modern mercantilism, led by China, then Biden and Trump), a philosophical change that will last.

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: Europe is really sort of left behind because they don't really have a central government to deal with this environment and to compete
claims.claim: Europe is behind in a mercantilist world because it lacks a central government, though Germany's defence initiative is unintentionally fiscal stimulus for the European economy.

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: we don't have like a single decision maker doing trades we work in groups to understand the world, to do research together, to formulate plans for managing money in the markets
claims.claim: Bridgewater's systematic fundamental process avoids a single decision-maker; research and plans are made in groups as a team effort.

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: after 40 years compounding at 10% versus 5% the the terminal value is six times
claims.claim: Compounding a small difference in annual rate (10% vs 5%) is trivial at 10 years but sixfold at 40 years, so long horizons magnify skill differences; play the long game.

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: It's got theories based on assumptions that are not true
claims.claim: Economics textbooks rest on false assumptions and no book explains how the world works, so one must ask own questions and find own answers from data, books and people.

claims.speaker: Bob Prince
claims.quote: I'm advising this utility on how to manage their debt structure against their their business you know and we it was very successful
claims.claim: A company can hedge its embedded market exposures on the liability side by structuring its debt (currency, maturity, rate type) to offset what its business revenues are exposed to, as Bridgewater did for BC Hydro.
claims.conditions: business with large market-driven revenue exposure and sizeable debt
claims.testable: partly - hedge effectiveness can be measured case by case

claims.speaker: Noah Yechiely
claims.quote: primary objective is um producing return that is uncorrelated
claims.claim: A true hedge fund aims for returns uncorrelated with the market, which helps a portfolio because the stream rises when other assets fall; many so-called hedge funds are simply long-only.
claims.indicator: correlation of fund returns with market
claims.direction: add uncorrelated return stream to portfolio
claims.conditions: Benefit appears when other assets are falling
claims.testable: yes - correlation of fund returns to market is measurable

claims.speaker: Noah Yechiely
claims.quote: selling a beta or selling regular IR regular returns that you can get in the market and they just charge more
claims.claim: Many hedge funds drifted into holding assets long because that earns market returns over time on which they can charge fees, so they sell beta, not unique returns.
claims.conditions: Because uncorrelated return is hard to produce
claims.testable: yes - regress hedge fund returns on market factors

claims.speaker: Noah Yechiely
claims.quote: markets are very efficient it's very hard to make uh money in markets
claims.claim: Markets are very efficient: the whole hedge fund industry earns a few billion, a few basis points on hundreds of trillions of assets, because competing smart participants make uncorrelated returns hard.
claims.indicator: hedge fund industry profit relative to market size
claims.testable: partly - industry-level argument, efficiency claim is general

claims.speaker: Noah Yechiely
claims.quote: particular niches in the market that are inefficient and there are there are reasons why they would be inefficient
claims.claim: Good hedge funds exploit niches that are inefficient for structural reasons, but the returns and capacity there are small.
claims.testable: partly - capacity-limited niche alpha hard to test

claims.speaker: Noah Yechiely
claims.quote: some strategies tend to work become public um many investors are following them and when you have many investors trying to chase the same U the same thing the returns are falling
claims.claim: Once a strategy becomes public and many investors follow it, its returns fall.
claims.testable: yes - compare returns before and after publication or crowding

claims.speaker: Noah Yechiely
claims.quote: data that was not available it was only available to a particular handful of people
claims.claim: Data and analysis tools once available to a few are now public and cheap, so data- and technology-dependent edges in markets have become more efficient.
claims.testable: partly - alpha decay by data availability can be examined

claims.speaker: Noah Yechiely
claims.quote: how much spending is in the market how much the economy is growing inflation and micro forces that are shifting the entire asset class together
claims.claim: Top-down macro investing targets aggregate forces (spending, growth, inflation) that move whole asset classes together, while bottom-up stock picking on company quality is neutralised when you hold both Boeing and Airbus.
claims.direction: long or short asset classes on macro drivers
claims.testable: partly - framework, depends on indicator chosen

claims.speaker: Noah Yechiely
claims.quote: trying to figure out why things are happening rather than trying to see what worked in the past
claims.claim: Successful investors understand the causal drivers of markets rather than following what worked in the past.

claims.speaker: Noah Yechiely
claims.quote: always assume that you're wrong rather than that you're right
claims.claim: Investors should challenge their own beliefs and, when a strategy shows a high Sharpe ratio, ask why it works and whether it will continue as in the past.

claims.speaker: Noah Yechiely
claims.quote: but all assets tends to go up and down together they are correlated
claims.claim: Long-only assets tend to rise over time as payment for providing capital, but they are mostly correlated with each other, so a long-only mix gives limited diversification and an uncorrelated return stream is what adds most to a portfolio.
claims.direction: long assets earn a premium over time
claims.testable: yes - cross-asset correlations and long-run asset returns are measurable

claims.speaker: Noah Yechiely
claims.quote: some of the markets became more efficient some of the markets became less efficient um and the efficiency also moves from one thing to the other
claims.claim: Market efficiency is not uniformly rising: some markets have become more efficient, others less, and inefficiency migrates from one area to another over time, so where edges exist must be reassessed.
claims.testable: partly - decay or revival of strategy returns by market and period can be measured

claims.speaker: Noah Yechiely
claims.quote: the approach how you break down the problem into its pieces how you build a framework to solve the problem how you find the data
claims.claim: Investment research is the same analytical process as consulting or engineering: break a new problem into pieces, build a framework, then find data to test it.

claims.speaker: Noah Yechiely
claims.quote: whether you know like our relationship with China where the tariffs will be higher lower how it will play out
claims.claim: Politics and geopolitics (e.g. US-China relations and whether tariffs go higher or lower) affect every company and market, so even bottom-up investors must understand the macro and political forces acting on their holdings.
claims.testable: partly - tariff-news sensitivity of stocks can be measured

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: the stock market went up a lot
claims.claim: When the US ended gold convertibility on Aug 15 1971 (and Roosevelt in 1933), a devaluation of money pushed equities up sharply, the opposite of what Dalio expected.
claims.direction: long equities after a currency devaluation
claims.conditions: fiat currency devaluation by a debtor government

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: they devalue the dollar and stocks go down we have this inflationary
claims.claim: In 1973 the dollar devaluation, inflation and the oil crisis combined to push stocks down, showing that devaluation effects depend on whether inflation follows.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: pain plus reflection equals progress
claims.claim: Treat losses as signals: reflect on how reality works and codify a principle, which turns mistakes into improved rules.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: August 1982 um was the exact bottom in the stock market the Dow was at 777
claims.claim: Dalio correctly called the 1982 EM debt default but wrongly predicted a depression; policy easing made Aug 1982 the exact equity bottom, so being right on events does not mean being right on market direction.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: diversification properly done could reduce my Risk by up to 80% without reducing my return
claims.claim: Combining good, uncorrelated bets can cut portfolio risk by up to 80% without lowering expected return.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: confidently thinking they're ro right without stress testing their thinking with the smartest people
claims.claim: Stress test views with the smartest people who disagree, since confidence without challenge is the main source of decision error.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: most of the things that surprised me were due to them not happening in my lifetime but that they happened many times in history
claims.claim: Surprises come from events not seen in a lifetime but common in history, so study history whenever something big and new happens.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: that understanding of History led me to be able to anticipate the 2008 financial crisis
claims.claim: Studying the 1930s let Dalio anticipate the 2008 crisis and Bridgewater made money when most lost.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: the amounts of debt creation and debt monetization that whole dynamic and last time that happened was in 1930 to 45 period
claims.claim: Current debt creation and monetization, internal left-right conflict and rising-power conflict mirror 1930-45, when a debt-driven depression caused internal and external fights for power.
claims.conditions: large debt, wealth and values gaps, rising power challenging dominant one

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: that Confluence of those forces that we're talking about these five great forces
claims.claim: Over 500 years of reserve-currency empires, five forces (debt, internal conflict, external conflict, acts of nature, technology) recur and drive rises and declines.
claims.testable: partly - 500 years historical, few data points

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: Debt Service becomes a higher and higher percentage of your expenses
claims.claim: As debt accumulates, debt service takes a rising share of spending and squeezes out consumption, a self-compounding mechanic.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: if you don't have a return in relation to inflation that is High Enough by holding that debt you won't hold that debt
claims.claim: If bond returns do not compensate for inflation, holders will not hold the debt, so it falls to central banks to buy.
claims.direction: real yield too low causes bond selling and central bank buying

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: if you give out a lot of money to a lot of people a lot more money they're going to spend a lot more money
claims.claim: COVID-era governments sent out more money than the income losses, on top of negative interest rates and central bank bond buying, which pulled inflation up.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: all the central banks have lost a lot of money a lot of money equivalent roughly for most central banks on average 8% of GDP
claims.claim: Central banks that bought bonds now hold losses of about 8% of GDP on average and need recapitalization by governments (UK about 2% of GDP), which increases deficits in a self-reinforcing loop.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: what the central bank is forced to choose between is interest rates Rising a lot
claims.claim: With old and new debt both unwanted, the central bank must choose between sharply higher rates, which hurt everything, or printing more money.
claims.conditions: large selling of old debt plus large deficits

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: we're also seeing the possibility of sanctioning their debt
claims.claim: Like Japan before WWII (oil embargo, frozen assets), the US now uses chip embargoes and possible debt sanctions on China as economic war, as part of the great-power conflict.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: the winner of a technology war is going to be the winner of this Global World Order war
claims.claim: Technology leadership (chips) determines who wins the broader world order contest.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: when you come into a conflict period there is autocracy or downright dictatorship
claims.claim: In conflict periods countries move toward autocracy and force internal alignment, as in WWII.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: 22% of American manufactured goods Imports come from China
claims.claim: Economic interdependence (22% of US manufactured imports from China) makes a full economic or military break extremely costly, which restrains both sides.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: we're not going to cross those red lines now but we are both sides preparing for that war
claims.claim: Both sides will press the edge of the Taiwan and chip red lines without crossing for now, but risks of conflict rise over time.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: are you earning more than you are spending so that your income statement is good and your balance sheet
claims.claim: Prefer countries with good income statements and balance sheets (savings, financial strength) when allocating geographically.
claims.testable: yes - country-selection backtest on balance-sheet data

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: you could lose more money money not just in price movements but you could be confiscated from you
claims.claim: Avoid places with extreme left-right internal conflict, where history shows losses beyond price moves, including confiscation.
claims.conditions: conflict over how to distribute money

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: the neutral countries have done better than even the winning countries in Wars economically
claims.claim: Neutral countries have done better economically than even winners of wars (Britain was bankrupted; the US entered late and accumulated gold), so favor neutral countries.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: India is emerging as a power um that is also remaining neutral
claims.claim: Dalio favors neutral, rising places such as ASEAN/Singapore, India and Gulf states (UAE, Saudi) while diversifying asset classes.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: that estimated amount is is between five and10 trillion dollar uh a year
claims.claim: Climate costs (energy transition, infrastructure, damage) are estimated at $5-10 trillion a year, about 5-10% of world GDP, which adds to fiscal deficit pressure.
claims.conditions: competes with other spending on infrastructure and education

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: tremendously productivity enhancing but it's a power also like nuclear power
claims.claim: AI raises productivity but disrupts who gains: inventors win and those replacing labor (robotics plus AI) shift wealth, which feeds political conflict.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: if I can have clear decision rules that I uh could then specify and see how they would have worked in the past such as the 1930s
claims.claim: Write explicit decision rules, back-test them on history (e.g. the 1930s), then put them into algorithms; rules learned from the 1930s made money in 2008.
claims.testable: yes - backtest rules on historical analogs

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: it could process a lot more complex things um instantaneously a lot quicker a lot less emotionally
claims.claim: Algorithms encoding decision rules process more complexity faster and less emotionally than humans, and can be tested on history; this was a key to Bridgewater success.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: I'm more believable in that so that believability weighted voting made sense
claims.claim: Weight votes by data-measured believability in each domain, creating an idea meritocracy rather than relying on authority.
claims.testable: partly - requires track records by person

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: rather than a buyer of the bonds they've turned into essentially a seller of those bonds
claims.claim: Central bank balance sheet runoff turns the Fed from a buyer into a seller of bonds, putting upward pressure on yields.
claims.conditions: low demand relative to supply of bonds

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: some countries believe it's risky to own particular us bonds because maybe they can get sanctioned
claims.claim: Sanctions risk lowers foreign demand for US Treasuries and other bonds, raising the risk premium on the higher-rate side as supply keeps rising.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: since I started going to China in 1984 per capita income increased by 28 times um the life expectancy increased by 10 years poverty rates went from
claims.claim: China's rise since 1984 (per-capita income up 28 times, life expectancy up 10 years, poverty from 88% to under 1%) is the economic base of a rising power that now challenges the existing world order, which in history leads to conflict.
claims.indicator: China per-capita income, life expectancy, poverty rate
claims.direction: rising power vs incumbent conflict risk up

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: if the United States says we're in favor of China of Taiwan Independence so what we are doing is there's a pushing of that limit
claims.claim: The one trigger both sides know would cause a war is the US backing Taiwan independence; election-period pledges to defend Taiwan and arms sales push toward that red line.
claims.indicator: US statements on Taiwan independence; arms sales
claims.direction: geopolitical risk up around US election
claims.testable: partly - event study on Taiwan-related announcements

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: the most important thing that United States can do or Western powers can do is be strong okay what does that mean strong financially strong working together being united being productive
claims.claim: Outcomes of the great-power contest depend on each side's internal strength (finances, unity, productivity), so internal debt and political conflict weaken a country's external position.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: you don't invest in um the um old Technologies the old energy sources so you have less Supply in that period of time before it's uh replaced by the newer energy sources
claims.claim: During the energy transition, underinvestment in old energy sources cuts supply before new sources replace them, making the transition costly (supply squeeze) on top of infrastructure and damage costs.

claims.speaker: Ray Dalio
claims.quote: they've all lost a lot of money and and it constitutes a high percentage of their portfolios
claims.claim: Investors already hold a large share of portfolios in bonds and have lost money on them, so demand for new bonds is weak relative to supply, and rates face upward pressure until the consequences are felt in the economy.
claims.indicator: bond share of portfolios; supply vs demand
claims.testable: partly - holdings data vs term premium

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: the three big themes that I'm concerned about or focused on are a the change in how the global and US economy uh is being managed
claims.claim: Three macro themes: a shift to modern mercantilism (reaction to China's rise), the AI technology revolution, and record concentration of capital in US equities and illiquid assets.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: capital is more concentrated in the US than ever, more concentrated in equity and illquid assets. Um so a kind of risky setup.
claims.claim: Capital concentration in US assets is a risk factor, so understanding where money has flowed, why, and how likely it is to reverse matters.
claims.indicator: global capital allocation to US assets
claims.testable: partly - foreign holdings of US assets data

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: a major change in the 1980s, a shift towards small government, a lot of capitalism
claims.claim: Regime shift analogy: the 1980s turn to small government and free markets is now being replaced by mercantilism (tariffs, state control, trade as zero-sum), so investors must adapt rather than assume the old economy.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: You would have thought that people would have taken down their massive risk concentration in the US because it's changing so quickly.
claims.claim: Expected effect of mercantilism: a higher risk premium on US assets and diversification away from the US; muted at the index level because AI offsets.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: the worst performance of US equities relative to the rest of the world equities in common currency terms that you've had over that 15-ear period
claims.claim: Under calm index averages, US equities posted their worst relative performance vs the world in 15 years, so averages hide stress visible in sub-components (US ex-AI, gold).
claims.indicator: US vs world equity relative return in common currency; gold

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: everything looks fine on the surface. If you look underneath that, split up the equity market.
claims.claim: Look beneath index averages (e.g. S&P ex-AI names, gold) to see shifts the headline averages hide.
claims.indicator: S&P 500 ex-AI vs rest of world; gold

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: take all of your human intuition, translate that into um algorithms
claims.claim: Bridgewater's method: write down beliefs, stress-test them, and encode human intuition into algorithms (an expert system).

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: when will machines write the rules not just support the rules which we've been doing
claims.claim: Bridgewater built an AI agent investor (started 2022, producing alpha by 2024) run as a separate entity to generate independent ideas; machines learning rules rather than copying human intuition.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: I used to say the bubble's ahead of us, not behind us.
claims.claim: AI: bubble is ahead, not behind - in the early phase people underestimated how much will be invested.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: It's not a capex cycle that's the same as other capex cycles. This money is going to get spent, right?
claims.claim: AI capex is driven by strategic, non-profit motives of firms whose businesses are threatened, so spending persists beyond normal ROI discipline.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: we are in a more dangerous phase
claims.claim: Current AI phase is a resource grab (power, chips, scientists) where compounding must continue in the physical world, a more dangerous but not bubble phase.
claims.indicator: AI capex; power and chip supply

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: the depreciation schedule is probably going to be quite fast
claims.claim: Risk: AI-generated efficiency gains will obsolete current chips and assets quickly (fast depreciation).

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: This is how they're going to get their revenue. Not at all. Nvidia can get as much revenue as it wants.
claims.claim: Vendor financing is not bubble-style demand creation but Nvidia building a controlled ecosystem versus Google's full stack, with scarce chips as leverage.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: I think less than a thousand.
claims.claim: Cutting-edge AI scientists number under a thousand, making talent the binding constraint; poaching slows scientific progress.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: The US is no longer the US
claims.claim: Mercantilist shift: US no longer pursues international cooperation as before; the rest of the world has not retaliated against tariffs (picked off one by one), but is showing home bias and domestic investment.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: the biggest collapse in support for the United States in the rest of the world that we've ever seen
claims.claim: Collapse in US goodwill drives populist, mercantilist politics (shift to populist right then left), with less international cooperation.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: Two big things, right? You get tariffs
claims.claim: Mercantilism is inflationary: tariffs and resilient supply chains replace cheapest sourcing, reversing 30 years of productivity gains.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: there's nothing more inflationary really than military spending
claims.claim: Military spending is especially inflationary because it creates demand for labour and goods with no supply into the real economy; Germany and Europe are surging fiscal and defense spending.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: growth is dominated by this AI investment AI investment while starting to take up power capacity and whatever is very low
claims.claim: AI investment gives growth with low labour intensity, so growth is concentrated while the labour market is weak and the effect is initially disinflationary; AI adds ~1pt of 2% US growth.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: we think the fed is very comfortable above two and a half and probably we're in the three range as a base right now
claims.claim: Base case: US inflation about 3% for the next couple of years with Fed tolerant above 2.5%, versus breakeven near 2.25-2.5%.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: lowering real rates into a boom like this is particularly inflationary
claims.claim: Populist control of the central bank leading to lower real rates during an AI boom would be inflationary.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: we're all Brazil now
claims.claim: Fiscal-constraint thesis: developed economies (UK, soon US) are constrained like Brazil even with domestic currency debt; fiscal expansion in constrained countries lowers currency, equities and raises rates.
claims.direction: short gilts and currency of constrained countries; long unconstrained (Germany)

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: when you get constrained spending money becomes counterproductive rather than productive
claims.claim: Fiscal limits depend on domestic savings, productivity and willingness to hold your currency (Japan 300% debt vs Brazil 60-80%); beyond the limit, spending raises rates and hurts assets.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: how do we survive in the wide range of possible worlds rather than try to pick the best thing
claims.claim: Philosophy: survive across a wide range of worlds because compounding depends on avoiding bad outcomes.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: Most people have moved away from diversification because it hasn't worked for 15 years.
claims.claim: US-only equity concentration is a trap after 15 years of success; build a much more globally diversified portfolio.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: companies that directly compete between Europe and the US, they're generally priced cheap
claims.claim: Europe is investable: fiscal shift supports domestic profits, shareholder returns improved, and companies are cheaper than US peers with better earnings and management.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: the biggest risk of being invested in China is your government saying you can't be invested in China
claims.claim: China matters for diversification; its leadership moved to support the private sector and equity market to compete on AI; main risk is political access.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: All of a sudden the correlation between bonds and equities and currency will shift when you hit limits.
claims.claim: Bonds are no longer the 30-year diversifier because fiscal limits shift correlations, and fiscal policy responds to disinflation, so bonds do not hedge deflation as well.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: you're going to have this big competition for capital between fiscal and AI
claims.claim: Massive fiscal supply plus AI ecosystem spending (tech firms turning from net savers to spenders, private credit) creates a shortage of capital, pushing real rates up, opposed by US central bank pressure.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: this is not very helpful technology
claims.claim: Crypto: use cases mostly speculation, attracts corruption; Bitcoin has some merit as non-government money and gold substitute, but AI is a better bet.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: you have to do that by compounding understanding
claims.claim: Bridgewater's edge: understand the global financial system deeply and build portfolios, by writing down beliefs and compounding knowledge in human- and machine-readable form with a record of every change.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: If that knowledge is not in what we call our secure garden
claims.claim: Enforcement rule: research counts only when translated into compounded knowledge (plain-English reasoning plus code).

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: the reasoning is written and the manifestation of that reasoning in code exists and otherwise you get no credit for it
claims.claim: One common platform for all research in place of mixed tools makes research replicable and lets AI audit the rules.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: I wanted ya to be uncorrelated to pure alpha
claims.claim: AI venture run separately, designed around AI rather than humans, to avoid copying human flaws and get an uncorrelated alpha source; now being merged back.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: One of the reasons that AI hasn't swept through corporate America is people keep trying to replace humans with it
claims.claim: AI adoption works when processes are redesigned around the technology rather than replicating human tasks (Amazon robots example).

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: the reason we survived was partially this process that I'm saying is good and you make good decisions, but much more important is risk control
claims.claim: Survival over 50 years came mainly from risk control, accepting that all are flawed.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: we totally screwed it up because we were trying to systemize
claims.claim: COVID lesson: trying to systemise a unique shock made the model slow; Bridgewater now accelerates new research into positions before it is fully systematized and gives researchers independence (a controlled override).
claims.conditions: novel shocks with no systematic analogue

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: Barely but yes.
claims.claim: Overruling the system helps barely on average, so it is done rarely and with discipline.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: you have to know the future better than other people do in otherwise you should just be at the benchmark
claims.claim: Markets are a probabilistic game requiring being wrong often but right more; poker skills (incomplete information, probability, handling mistakes) transfer; machines surpassed humans in poker, an analogy for edge when machines learn faster than humans.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: you have to fight against certain human things
claims.claim: Radical transparency with feedback aimed up at leaders, and measuring that managers elicit criticism, lets best ideas win.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: The worst managers in the company are the ones that their people say all good things about.
claims.claim: Managers who get the most negative feedback are best, as it shows independent thinking is drawn out.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: I thought it would have bigger impact than it has as an example
claims.claim: Admission: the impact of mercantilism on markets has been smaller than he expected, partly explained by AI offset.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: being in unwilling to say what they believe or being unwilling to listen to other people
claims.claim: Hiring: balance open-mindedness and assertiveness; two failure modes are not speaking up and not listening.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: pain plus reflection equals progress
claims.claim: Ray Dalio's principle: reflect on pain to make progress; Dalio's succession took 15 years.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: we centralized the decision-m largely at the CIO level
claims.claim: Hardest decision: moving from CIO-centralised decisions to independent investors, requiring removal of long-tenured people from the process.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: all these investments have a Jc curve in the first [L340] phase you don't get you spend a lot of resources you don't get a lot of output other than the investment itself
claims.claim: AI investment follows a J-curve: in the first phase it absorbs large resources with little output beyond the investment itself, and only later becomes strongly disinflationary, so the disinflation is further out than many assume.
claims.testable: partly - capex share vs measured productivity over time

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: above potential two two and a like two and a half kind of percent growth and um and but a lot of that one and a half percent or so is going to be AI
claims.claim: Forecast: US growth next year a little above potential at about 2.5%, with roughly 1.5 points from AI investment, producing a two-track economy of a concentrated AI boom alongside a weak labour market.
claims.indicator: US real GDP growth, AI investment contribution
claims.direction: US growth above potential, labour weak
claims.conditions: AI capex continues; European fiscal push
claims.testable: yes - compare with realised GDP and investment contributions

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: for a while you're going to have this very divided Fed and where the chairman may be in the minority
claims.claim: View: a new Fed chair aligned with the administration may be outvoted often next year, giving a divided Fed until more aligned governors are appointed, a policy-uncertainty source.
claims.indicator: FOMC dissents / votes against the chair
claims.conditions: politically appointed chair with board not yet aligned
claims.testable: partly - dissent counts and rate volatility around FOMC

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: I think we're in this death march on institutions you've already seen that the World Trade Organization what does it even do now
claims.claim: International institutions (e.g. WTO) have lost their function and US domestic institutions are weakening fast, part of why the US is becoming a less exceptional, higher-risk-premium place to invest.
claims.direction: higher risk premium on US assets
claims.testable: no - institutional quality is hard to measure

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: interest rates have risen and real interest rates have risen such that there is a place for bonds in portfolios
claims.claim: After many investors left bonds at zero rates, the rise in nominal and real yields means bonds again deserve a place in portfolios, though with weaker diversification than in the past 30 years.
claims.conditions: starting yields well above zero; less useful where fiscal limits bind
claims.testable: yes - bond forward returns conditional on starting real yield

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: because that's all systemized they could just focus on what we're missing what is happening in the world today that you're worried that process doesn't have reflected
claims.claim: Research method: once accumulated understanding is fully systematised, the human research team (a couple hundred people) can concentrate only on what the systematic process does not yet capture, such as new regimes like modern mercantilism.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: we had done work on the 1917 Spanish flu, but the economic impact of the Spanish flu because it was so disperate was so different than what ended up happening and we knew it
claims.claim: Caveat on historical analogies: Bridgewater's systematic COVID response leaned on the Spanish flu precedent even though they knew its economic impact differed, so a known-imperfect analogue embedded in process can override better current knowledge.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: a paradigm of massive globalization, integration around the world. The US is a security umbrella to everything.
claims.claim: The last 15 years rested on globalisation, US security umbrella and deflationary easy money, making a plain S&P 500 the best asset; investment returns over decades are driven by such secular paradigms.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: we've called the new environment modern mercantalism meant to describe kind of a worldview that the state's job is to really maximize that country's its national wealth
claims.claim: The new regime, modern mercantilism, treats trade deficits as wealth transfers, pursues self-sufficiency and treats allies coercively, implying a different environment for assets.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: Markets have barely started pricing in.
claims.claim: The new paradigm is only starting to be priced, with prices still assuming the old one, so tariff headlines will be noisy but the change is fundamental.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the flip side of a massive trade deficit is a huge amount of current account inflows
claims.claim: US reliance on current account inflows, mostly from allies, means reduced foreign appetite for US assets cannot unwind in a day; policy of self-sufficiency pushes capital to stay at home (Germany defence example).

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: It fell by two Mexicos
claims.claim: After DeepSeek, Nvidia's market cap fell by roughly two Mexicos in a day, showing how under-capitalised markets like Mexico and Brazil are in world indices and the case for taking geographic diversification seriously.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: extremely vulnerable to a world where the US doesn't just keep beating everyone
claims.claim: Market-cap-guided investors are concentrated in the US; true diversification means markets with different growth, inflation, monetary policy and elections (Latin America, Asia).

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: I think there's very clearly some degree of economic slowdown ahead of us and some inflation ahead of us because of the set of policies.
claims.claim: Policies imply some slowdown and some inflation in the US; most portfolios are not prepared and have shrinking liquid allocations to respond or take advantage of pricing opportunities.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: 25 is where you get the pain from the tariffs. 26 is where you can actually get the fiscal stimulation
claims.claim: Tariff pain is expected in 2025 and fiscal stimulation and reshoring in 2026; faster resolution of uncertainty speeds reshoring.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: I like fixed income a lot more in other countries in the United States
claims.claim: Prefer non-US government bonds because other central banks can ease more straightforwardly while the Fed faces an inflation impulse from tariffs.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: If you're in other countries, it's much more deflationary, right?
claims.claim: Tariff effects are inflationary in the US (more so if supply constraints) but deflationary abroad (weaker currencies, lower energy), so the Fed cannot ease easily while other central banks can, and little non-US easing is priced.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: you kind of started this environment with nothing really looking like a big risk premium on treasuries
claims.claim: Part of the Treasury yield backup is investors demanding a risk premium that was close to nil when the episode began.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: in some of these fixed income markets it's like a once every 101 15 year type size
claims.claim: A systematic measure of pressure relative to history shows non-US fixed income and big currency crosses (euro, yen) at once-in-10-to-15-year extremes, which supports positions.
claims.direction: long non-US government bonds; long euro and yen vs USD

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: lots of the big currency drivers don't work that way. They're going to take a while to work through governance.
claims.claim: The dollar fall so far reflects speculative and fast money; slow drivers such as official and institutional flows move gradually, so shorting the dollar against euro and yen is attractive.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: my answer would be it's not the best time ever take risk but mostly take it outside the United States
claims.claim: How much risk and where is the key question; take moderate risk, mostly outside the United States.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: being able to also profit from the fact the economy has actually been weak, the bonds have been a good buy, that the currency have devalued
claims.claim: Expressing a country view across stocks, bonds and currencies lets one profit from China even when stocks do not do well; the China-only and ex-China funds were biggest winners in 2025.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the vast majority of investors when they go into a country, they just buy the stock market
claims.claim: Most investors express country views only through stocks; there is no reason to invest that way, and flexibility across asset classes is an advantage.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: you tend to get depending where you are in the risk spectrum something much more similar to equity-like risk
claims.claim: Fixed income capabilities were hollowed out in a zero-rate world as money moved to private credit, which carries equity-like risk rather than uncorrelated alpha.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: duration and currency are great alpha spaces that have seemed uninteresting for a while where rates were zero and are kind of coming back in a big way
claims.claim: With rates no longer zero, duration and currency selection across countries offer uncorrelated alpha again, though many mandates are limited to US Treasuries.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: You're clearly looking at a world that has more inflation risk than it used to.
claims.claim: Commodities, including gold, are ignored but useful assets in a world with more inflation risk.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: everybody's long and oil I think people are short
claims.claim: Tactically prefer gold to oil: gold is crowded long after a big run, oil is crowded short and could spike.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: There's so many zero correlated opportunity assets out there relative to how underutilize that.
claims.claim: Many uncorrelated opportunities exist outside the benchmark holdings, so portfolios should ask what diversifies what they hold.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: keep beating what you got before is even stronger
claims.claim: Starting prices already assume the old paradigm continues: unlike 2010, when prices embedded low US profitability, current prices assume US companies keep beating past results, so a shift in paradigm has more room to hurt US assets.
claims.indicator: US profitability expectations embedded in prices
claims.direction: US equities vulnerable to paradigm shift
claims.testable: partly - implied profitability expectations can be compared with 2010

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: I particularly like currencies in places like Brazil and Mexico
claims.claim: Karniol-Tambour likes Brazilian and Mexican currencies as part of Latin American exposure, and sees capital staying at home as the US pushes self-sufficiency.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the last 48 hours or so have taken some tail risk off the table
claims.claim: The May 2025 tariff de-escalation removed the tail risk of massive factory shutdowns and empty shelves, but a slowdown and some inflation still lie ahead, which most portfolios are not prepared for.
claims.testable: no - view on a specific episode

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: an inflationary impulse from the tariffs is a one-off. It kind of goes through like a VAT tax increase and fades
claims.claim: The Fed's hope is that tariff inflation is a one-off price-level shift like a VAT rise, but if tariffs come with supply disruption it looks more like Covid, with demand intact and supply short, and persistent inflation; this uncertainty stops the Fed from easing.
claims.conditions: depends on whether tariffs create supply problems
claims.testable: partly - core inflation response after tariff shocks

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: look, Chinese stocks are extremely cheap and you got to think about valuation and there's certainly a path where they stimulate and you get something out of the stocks, but it's not the only scenario
claims.claim: Chinese equities are very cheap and could rally on stimulus, but this is only one scenario, so Bridgewater earns in China through weak-economy exposures too (bonds, currency devaluation).
claims.direction: long Chinese stocks possible on stimulus

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: if there's a recession at least I'll get some easing and that'll be kind of balancing out of all my risky assets
claims.claim: Institutions held fixed income as a recession hedge (central banks ease when growth falls); when rates were at zero that role seemed pointless, so money moved to private credit with equity-like risk, hollowing out bond-selection capability.
claims.indicator: bonds as recession hedge via central-bank easing
claims.conditions: fails when rates are at zero and cannot fall
claims.testable: partly - bond returns in recessions by starting rate level

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: for a business to grow its profit margin it has to simply raise revenue or get people to pay for its products without paying labor
claims.claim: Aggregate corporate profit exists only if spending exceeds wage income, so profits are financed by borrowing, dissaving or government deficits rather than by wages.
claims.indicator: US corporate profits relative to GDP
claims.direction: corporate profits up when spending funded by non-wage sources
claims.conditions: for the whole economy, not a single firm
claims.testable: partly - profit share vs credit/deficit/savings flows is measurable

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: most importantly leverage borrowing spending down your savings and so for example households can go and take out a mortgage put on their credit card use their savings
claims.claim: Household borrowing and savings drawdown are channels that let workers buy goods without earning the money, which inflates corporate profits.
claims.direction: profits up when household leverage or dissaving rises
claims.testable: partly - household credit and saving rate series exist

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: businesses can do the same thing when they create capital expenditures because often they go and borrow to do those capital expenditures
claims.claim: Debt-financed corporate capex creates revenue for equipment sellers with no wage payout, so it also supports aggregate profits.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the government can increase the deficit and reduce the deficit
claims.claim: Government deficits supply income that is not paid out as wages, so larger deficits raise corporate profits and smaller deficits cut them.
claims.testable: partly - deficit vs profit share is testable

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: in the decades leading up to the financial crisis basically you had very significant secular forces
claims.claim: Before 2008, secular forces (globalization, deregulation, fewer unions) drove the structural rise in profit share.
claims.testable: no - narrative of structural forces, no sharp signal

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: a lot of deregulation the fact that there are fewer and fewer labor unions you basically had these structural forces that reduced a lot of workers bargaining power
claims.claim: Globalization, deregulation and union decline cut worker bargaining power, so wages lagged and workers borrowed to keep spending, raising profits.
claims.direction: wage share down, profit share up
claims.testable: partly - wage share and union density are measurable

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: saving dollars drove interest rates down and that whole process of lowering the interest rates interest
claims.claim: Emerging-market and oil-producer dollar saving pushed rates down for years, which let private borrowers keep funding spending that supported profits.
claims.indicator: EM and oil exporter reserve accumulation, interest rates

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: a lot of the borrowing that was done whether it's housing and subprime couldn't really be done anymore
claims.claim: After the financial crisis private-sector leveraging ended and the government took over as the source of non-wage spending.
claims.direction: private leverage down, government deficit up

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: lots of money is printed lots of people get that money but really drives up financial assets and wealthy people own financial assets disproportionately
claims.claim: QE mostly lifts financial assets owned by the wealthy, who spend little of the gain, so it supports demand weakly per dollar and raises inequality.
claims.direction: financial assets up, spending boost small
claims.testable: partly - marginal propensity to spend by wealth bucket

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: corporate profits actually surged to new highs now that doesn't usually happen
claims.claim: In 2020 profits rose to record highs while the economy collapsed, an unusual disconnect between profits and activity.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the government gave people a significant amount of money that actually more than offsets all the wages that they lost
claims.claim: Direct fiscal transfers that exceeded lost wages let households keep spending while firms cut payroll, the ideal setup for record profits.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the bottom 60 or 80 of households had the fastest healing and balance sheets we've ever seen
claims.claim: Stimulus checks repaired household balance sheets very fast, which left households able to spend from savings later.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the last couple months not many months but two three months of spending have been totally totally funded by households basically dis saving
claims.claim: With transfers gone, spending is being funded by lower saving rates and credit card borrowing, which cannot be sustained to push profits higher.
claims.indicator: personal saving rate, credit card borrowing
claims.direction: spending growth down once dissaving ends
claims.testable: yes - saving rate and card credit are published

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: rates are rising and we already have the biggest rise in mortgage rates in decades very very fast very very rapid falling asset prices this isn't going to be the time that households choose
claims.claim: Rising rates and falling asset prices make households unlikely to lever up or save less again, so debt cannot fill the gap left by fiscal support.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: we now have the tightest labor market in decades companies everywhere are raising wages and especially for lower incomes
claims.claim: A very tight labor market has shifted bargaining power to workers, raising wages for the lowest incomes and squeezing profit margins.
claims.direction: wage share up, profit margin down

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: we're really unlikely to get another push against corporate bargaining power from things like new globalization we've already globalized every good we could globalize
claims.claim: The globalization tailwind to margins is exhausted, so no new push against labor bargaining power is available.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: every possible political proposal to address inequality in some way says maybe you should raise corporate taxes they're the lowest they've been in decades
claims.claim: Corporate taxes and antitrust regulation are at multi-decade lows, so political pressure on inequality points toward higher taxes and tougher regulation, a profit headwind.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: there are particular areas like fuel and oil and gas and food that are specifically inelastic and specifically have inflation
claims.claim: Inflation concentrated in inelastic items such as fuel and food squeezes the budgets of the bottom 40-60% of consumers, so non-commodity firms cannot raise prices.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: back then about 30 of the stock market was commodity producers today it's more like 3
claims.claim: In the 1970s about 30% of the stock market was commodity producers who benefited from inflation, now only about 3%, so equities benefit far less from commodity inflation today.
claims.indicator: commodity producer weight in equity index
claims.direction: index profits benefit less from inflation

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: today we're telling companies well maybe you want to spend actually for the resilience of your supply chain
claims.claim: Spending on supply-chain resilience and decarbonization is low-return capex, so it will not lift profits like past investment.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: if interest rates rose one and a half percent on a 10-year bond and maybe you have a 10-year stream of earnings that's a 15 equity decline
claims.claim: Back-of-envelope duration: a 1.5 point rise in the 10-year yield on a 10-year earnings stream implies about a 15% equity decline.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: equities have basically fallen in line with the fact that rates have risen that's it that's all that happens
claims.claim: Equities have only repriced for higher rates, not for lower profits, so no earnings slowdown is priced in.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the market is not expecting a very significant slowdown or a very significant change in the path of earnings for companies
claims.claim: The market embeds a goldilocks scenario of little slowdown, so a profit decline is a downside risk to equities.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: people demanded a higher risk free to be in stocks in an inflationary environment it was harder to control all that
claims.claim: High inflation makes the economy more volatile and raises the required return on stocks, which hurt equities in the 1970s even though profits held up.
claims.direction: equity valuations down when inflation high
claims.testable: yes - inflation regimes vs equity multiples

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: u.s companies are expected to continue doing better than any other companies in the rest of the world
claims.claim: Priced-in US outperformance requires still higher profitability or more market share, and prior decades of single-country success rarely repeat.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: u.s corporate profits are currently at the highest level they've really ever been
claims.claim: US corporate profits relative to GDP stand at multi-decade, record highs in mid-2022, which is the starting point for the argument that they are exposed to mean reversion.
claims.indicator: US corporate profits as a share of GDP
claims.direction: record profit share is a downside risk for equities
claims.testable: yes - NIPA corporate profits / GDP series

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: that's a mechanical answer right these are all people governments individuals businesses they have to choose to borrow for a reason
claims.claim: The profit identity (profits need non-wage spending) is only a mechanical accounting condition; whether households, firms and governments actually choose to borrow or deficit-spend depends on behavioural and structural drivers, so the forecast has to model why they would.
claims.conditions: identity holds always; the funding sources are choices that can stop
claims.testable: partly - sectoral financial balances are measurable, motives are not

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: they did a lot of savings also put a lot of money into stock market and crypto
claims.claim: Part of the 2020-21 stimulus transfers was saved or put into stocks and crypto, so fiscal money also inflated risk-asset prices while the rest kept consumer spending (and so corporate revenue) going.
claims.indicator: household savings, retail equity and crypto flows after stimulus
claims.direction: fiscal transfers push up risk assets
claims.testable: yes - retail flows and savings rate around stimulus payments

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: rates were already zero it was sort of a breaking point of the paradigm
claims.claim: Before Covid the profit-support paradigm was at its limit: profits and inequality were at extremes, QE had been used and rates were already at zero, so monetary policy had no room left to extend the leverage-driven profit model.
claims.indicator: profit share, inequality, policy rates at zero
claims.conditions: rates at the zero bound, extreme inequality and profit share

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: this insane boom that all these checks set off and the fact that everyone could spend so much money is creating inflation
claims.claim: The transfer-fuelled spending boom created inflation, which forced central banks to raise rates, and that rate rise in turn closes the borrowing channel that was supporting profits, so the stimulus sows the end of its own profit support.
claims.indicator: inflation, policy and mortgage rates after fiscal stimulus
claims.direction: inflation then tightening then lower household borrowing
claims.conditions: large demand stimulus into constrained supply
claims.testable: partly - sequence is observable, causality is judgement

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: we know what happens with the lag and we know that it's coming
claims.claim: The damage from rising rates and falling asset prices to household borrowing and spending operates with a lag and has not yet shown up in spending data, so a spending slowdown is still ahead.
claims.indicator: lagged effect of rate rises on household spending and borrowing
claims.direction: spending and profits slow after tightening
claims.conditions: after a fast rise in mortgage rates and asset-price falls
claims.testable: yes - lead-lag of rate changes and consumption/credit growth

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: you could think about a stock as just a series of cash flows discounted for today
claims.claim: A stock can be decomposed into expected profits plus a discount rate made of the risk-free interest rate and the risk premium for waiting, so one can read from prices what is priced in: here the price move matches the discount-rate change, not an earnings change.
claims.indicator: discounted cash flow split into profits, interest rate and risk premium
claims.conditions: public equities where prices reveal what is priced in
claims.testable: yes - decompose index returns into rate, premium and earnings expectation changes

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: profits are extremely high and it seems very unlikely they can remain this high at unprecedented levels forever
claims.claim: Because all the funding sources of non-wage spending are fading and the structural margin tailwinds have reversed, record profit levels should revert downward, which makes lower earnings the central bearish forecast for US equities.
claims.indicator: profit share of GDP, corporate margins
claims.direction: short or underweight equities as profits mean-revert
claims.conditions: when the profit share is at a record and borrowing, deficits and labour weakness stop supporting it
claims.testable: yes - forward earnings versus starting profit share
